To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Au-MEOA-MA electrodes and the MA-anti MA antibody interactions are characterized with time constant dispersion, typical of grain/grain boundary phase, microstructure, and the Au-MEAD-MA electrodes, and the MA-antibody interactions, are characterized as microelectrodes with pinholes that permit electron transport.

we have demonstrated the ability of self-assembled monomolecular layers (SAMs) of MA, a major component of the mycobacterial cell wall, to discriminate between TB-positive and TB-negative human sera, and that this discrimination is based on the ability of the MA-SAMs to discriminate between the anti-MA antibodies present within the sera.

the electron transfer dynamics across self- assembled N-(2- mercaptoethyl)octa-decanamide/mycolicacid layers are governed by the presence of pinholes that permit electron transport from a redox-active species in solution to the underlying gold surface, and that anti- mycolic acid antibodies present in TB positive human sera strongly interact with the mycolic acid layer on a self-assembled N- (2-mercaptonethyl)octadocanamide monolayer
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of a potential impedimetrical biosensing platform for tuberculosis.

the development of a new impedimetric immunodiagnostic tool for active tuberculosis based on the use of self-assembled monomolecular layers of N-(2-Mercaptoethyl)octa-decanamide/mycolic acids as recognition elements.
the development of an impedimetric biosensing platform based on a self-assembled layer of MA antigens, which can be used for the detection of anti-MA antibodies from TB infected human sera.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Au-MEOA-MA layer is a microelectrode array with pinholes that act as microelectrodes and that the anti-MA antibody interacts with Au-MEOA and Au-MEOA-Ma layers in a similar manner.
the Au-MEDOA and Au-MEODOA-MA layers are microstructures with pinholes acting like microelectrodes.

the electrochemical impedance spectroscopic (EIS) approach is a useful tool to study the integrity of MA antigens integrated in a SAM of N-(2-Mercaptoethyl)octa-decanamide on gold electrodes, and the interaction of these MA antigens with anti-MA antibodies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Au-MEA-MA bio-interface is a very promising platform for TB detection.

we were able to use electrochemical impedance spectroscopic (EIS) techniques to probe the structure of a self-assembled layer of mycolic acids (MA) on a gold electrode, as well as to investigate the interaction of anti-MA antibodies with the MA layer.
, we have shown that MA can be successfully integrated in SAMs and the integrity and properties of the MA SAM can be interrogated using electrochemical techniques.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the MA-antibody interactions are characterized by a time-constant dispersion typical of microstructures that have grain/grain boundary phase, and that these crucial physico-electrical insights into the behaviour MA should provide a basis for the design of a potential impedimetirc immuno sensing platform for active TB.

the electrochemical impedance spectroscopic (EIS) technique is a powerful tool for probing the integrity and properties of MA antigens in the context of the design of impedimetric immunodevice for the diagnosis of TB.

the Au-MEA and Au-MEA-MA electrodes behave as microelectode arrays, with pinhole defects acting as the micro-electrodes that permit charge transfer between a redox active species in solution and the gold surface.
